summary: Defines a BGP-based auto-discovery mechanism for Layer-1 VPNs, letting provider edge devices find other edges with ports in the same VPN. That information is needed to complete signaling. It aims for single-end provisioning where adding a port needs changes only at one PE and one CE. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Think of a club where each branch must know the others. This lets branches announce themselves, so adding one new door does not require rewriting every list.

questions: what is bgp auto-discovery for l1vpn
what is a port information table
subtitle: How provider routers use BGP to discover which of them serve ports in the same Layer-1 VPN.

tldr.problem: Provider edge routers need to find the other edges that serve the same Layer-1 VPN, without every new port forcing configuration changes across the network.
tldr.mechanism: Each PE keeps a Port Information Table per VPN and advertises its local port tuples in BGP using a new address family (SAFI 69), with Route Targets controlling which PEs import what.
tldr.outcome: Only the PE with the new port and its attached CE need configuring (single-end provisioning), and no router has to hold all VPN information, but PEs must trust their BGP peers.

today: RFC 5195 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It covers only the basic mode of Layer-1 VPNs described in RFC 4847.

sections.title: Auto-Discovery for Layer-1 VPNs
sections.content:
A Layer-1 VPN (L1VPN) connects customer sites through a provider network. Before signaling can set up a connection, provider edge (PE) devices must discover which other PEs have ports attached to customer edge (CE) members of the same VPN. This RFC defines a BGP-based auto-discovery mechanism for that job.

The main objective is single-end provisioning: adding a port to an L1VPN should require configuration changes only on the PE that has the port and the CE connected to it.

Each PE advertises at least its own IP address and the list of <private address, provider address> tuples local to it. Remote PEs find the VPN members they share with the advertiser and use the information for address resolution during signaling. The RFC covers only the basic mode of L1VPN operation, not the enhanced mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Each door of a club tells all the other doors it exists. Then adding a new door means telling only the club, not rewriting everyone's list.

sections.title: Ports, Identifiers and Port Information Tables
sections.content:
A CE connects to a PE through one or more ports. Each CE port has a customer port identifier (CPI), unique within its L1VPN. Each PE port has a provider port identifier (PPI), unique within the provider network. Either may be an IPv4 or IPv6 address.

For every L1VPN with at least one port on a PE, the PE keeps a Port Information Table (PIT) holding <CPI, PPI> tuples for the ports in that VPN. A PIT may also hold routing information.

A PIT holds two kinds of data: local information about the CE ports attached to the PE (configured or learned from CEs), and remote information received from other PEs through auto-discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Each club keeps a notebook per team. It lists which door of the club matches which door of the team's members.

sections.title: Distributing Information with Route Targets
sections.content:
Local information is sent to other PEs using the BGP multiprotocol extensions of RFC 4760. To keep the data inside the right VPN, BGP route filtering uses the Route Target Extended Community from RFC 4360.

Each PIT is configured with one or more export Route Targets, used to tag local information as it enters the provider's BGP. The tagging can be as fine as a single <CPI, PPI> pair. Each PIT also has one or more import Route Targets, so only routes carrying at least one of them are imported.

When a provider adds a new L1VPN port to a PE, the port is associated with a PIT, and the PIT with that L1VPN, at provisioning time.

Because BGP works across autonomous systems, the mechanism could support L1VPNs spanning several ASs. Multi-AS L1VPNs are currently out of scope for the basic mode, and further work, including on security, may be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a colored sticker. A branch only keeps messages with a sticker color it was told to collect.

sections.title: Carrying L1VPN Information in BGP
sections.content:
The <CPI, PPI> mapping travels in the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes of RFC 4760, which announce and withdraw reachability. This RFC adds a new subsequent address family identifier (SAFI), Layer-1 VPN auto-discovery information, with value 69, and a new NLRI format.

The NLRI is a one-octet Length field followed by variable-length auto-discovery information, whose encoding is defined in a separate document (the L1VPN Basic Mode specification). If the Next Hop length is 4, the Next Hop is an IPv4 address; if it is 16, an IPv6 address.

Section 4 adds that the mechanism MAY also carry traffic engineering information for egress path selection, such as the switching capability and maximum LSP bandwidth of remote interfaces, using the BGP Traffic Engineering Attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages ride in an existing postal system with a new label, number 69, so everyone knows they are about doors.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content:
A PE that is not a route reflector keeps L1VPN information only if it has a VPN whose import Route Target matches one on the route. Otherwise it MUST discard the information, using inbound filtering. When a new import Route Target is added (a "VPN Join"), the PE MUST use the route refresh mechanism of RFC 2918 to reacquire what it discarded. When a target disappears (a "VPN Prune"), the PE MAY drop routes that no longer match. Join and Prune do not require BGP connections to be brought down.

As a result no PE needs all routes for all L1VPNs. Route reflectors can be partitioned among VPNs, P routers keep no VPN information, and with multi-hop EBGP the ASBRs need not hold any either. No single component limits the number of VPNs the network can support.

The RFC also notes a contrast with Internet routing: the Internet BGP system must carry all Internet routes and cannot be partitioned, while any number of independent BGP systems can carry VPN information.
sections.plainLanguage: Each branch only writes down news about its own teams, so nobody has to carry the whole world's list.

sections.title: Trust Between BGP Speakers
sections.content:
A PE MUST NOT be discovered as attached to a VPN unless it really is attached and authorized. If any node could send these advertisements and PEs accepted them, anyone could add any site to any L1VPN.

So a PE must trust its BGP peers, and trust that they secure their local attachments. For a direct BGP peer, the TCP MD5 authentication of RFC 2385 SHOULD be used. For information relayed through a chain of speakers, the trust relation MUST be transitive. BGP cannot tell whether information came from a speaker authorized to advertise it, so the procedures MUST be used only where adequate trust exists, such as within a single provider network.
sections.plainLanguage: The branches have to believe each other. If a stranger could join the announcements, they could add themselves to any team.

sections.title: IANA: SAFI 69
sections.content: The RFC assigns the new SAFI, Layer-1 VPN auto-discovery information, in the Subsequent Address Family Identifier registry using the Standards Action procedure. The value is 69.
sections.plainLanguage: The new message type got its own number, 69, in the official list of numbers.
